title: Quarto
text:
A .qmd with PHP cells needs no Quarto extension and no configuration beyond naming the kernel. Quarto’s jupyter engine starts the kernel, runs the cells in order, and puts each cell’s output into the document.
A cell is a fenced block whose info string is {php}, holding PHP without an opening tag:

title: Quarto
text:
Naming the kernel
jupyter: <name> is the form to use. Quarto resolves the name against the installed kernelspecs, so it is the --name that juphyter install was given.
---
jupyter: php85
---
Jupyter also writes a fuller block into a notebook, and Quarto accepts it in a .qmd. For juphyter it needs one field more than the three Jupyter writes:
---
jupyter:
  kernelspec:
    name: php85
    language: php
    display_name: "PHP 8.5"
    path: /Users/erik/Library/Jupyter/kernels/php85
---
path is the directory holding kernel.json. Quarto’s jupyter engine reads it when it looks beside a kernelspec for a quarto_setup_cell, which it does for any language it has no built-in support for, and jupyter: <name> is the only form that fills the field in by itself. Without path the render fails with KeyError: 'path'. Naming the kernel rather than describing it avoids the whole question.

title: Quarto
text:
Cell options
Quarto’s cell options are comments in the cell’s own language, written with a | after the comment marker. Quarto has no php entry in its comment-character table and falls back to #, which PHP reads as a line comment, so #| is a Quarto cell option and a PHP comment at once.
The options that matter most in a PHP document:

#| echo: false runs the cell and keeps its source out of the page.
#| eval: false shows the source and does not run it.
#| output: false runs the cell and shows no output.
#| error: true lets the render continue past a cell that throws, and keeps the traceback in the output.
#| fig-cap: "..." captions the cell’s figure.
#| label: fig-mileage gives the figure a cross-reference.

A captioned plot:

Plot::of(Datasets::mpg())->aes(x: 'cty', y: 'hwy')->point(opacity: 0.5);






City against highway mileage.


PHP cells come out syntax-highlighted. Pandoc’s PHP syntax definition expects a <?php opening tag, which a notebook cell has no place for, and it highlights the cell regardless.
Every render prints Unknown message type: 'comm_open' once, from ipykernel rather than from Quarto. The kernel installs no comm manager, which is the same absence that leaves ipywidgets unsupported, and the message has no effect on what is rendered.

title: Quarto
text:
What each format carries
A phiz plot publishes four representations and a phibble data frame publishes two. Each output format takes one of them, and Quarto’s choice is the same in every case: for HTML it prefers text/html, for LaTeX and Typst it prefers image/svg+xml, and it falls back to text/plain.








Format
A phiz plot
A phibble data frame




html
the interactive chart, drawn by Vega-Lite in the browser
the HTML table, with the dimensions and the type row


typst, pdf
the static SVG, placed as a numbered figure
a typeset table; the dimension note and the truncation footer are dropped


ipynb
the HTML embed
nothing: see below



Two consequences are worth knowing before you choose a format.
A PDF figure comes from the static SVG, which phiz produces by running the vl-convert binary. Install it from vl-convert’s releases and put it on PATH, or point PHIZ_VL_CONVERT at it. Without it a plot has no SVG and a PDF has no figure.
quarto render --to ipynb is a conversion of the rendered document rather than the notebook that was executed. Quarto keeps one representation per output and reaches ipynb through Pandoc’s Markdown reader. An HTML <table> does not survive that trip, so the output is dropped, and error outputs are dropped as well. This is Quarto’s conversion rather than anything about the kernel, and a stock python3 kernel loses an IPython.display.HTML('<table>...') output in exactly the same way. Render to HTML or to PDF when a document’s tables matter.

title: Quarto
text:
PDF output
Quarto produces a PDF through LaTeX or through Typst, and Typst is the easier of the two here. Typst ships inside Quarto and places an SVG as it is:
quarto render report.qmd --to typst
The LaTeX route needs one more tool. For LaTeX output Quarto also picks the SVG, and then has to convert it to a PDF, which it does with rsvg-convert from librsvg. Without that binary quarto render --to pdf stops with Could not convert a SVG to a PDF for output. Install librsvg, or render through Typst.

title: Quarto
text:
The kernel daemon
Quarto can keep a kernel alive between renders, which saves starting PHP and loading the project’s autoloader again. Two conditions have to hold, and for a PHP kernel today the second one does not:

The daemon has to be asked for. Quarto turns it on by default only in an interactive session outside CI, and --execute-daemon <seconds> or execute: daemon: <seconds> asks for it explicitly.
Quarto only keeps a kernel whose language it can write a setup or a cleanup cell for. It looks for lang/<language> among its own resources and then for a quarto_setup_cell or quarto_cleanup_cell file beside the kernelspec. It ships neither for PHP, and juphyter install writes neither, so the server exits after one render and the next render starts a new kernel.

The practical effect is that each render of a PHP document gets a fresh session, and nothing of a previous render is in scope. Setting
execute:
  daemon: false
makes that explicit, and is the setting to reach for if a future release starts daemonizing PHP kernels and a document turns out to depend on a fresh session. A document that declares a class or a function is such a document: PHP cannot redeclare either, so a second render against a kept-alive kernel would fail on the cell that declares it.
The engine is ready for the daemon whenever Quarto starts using it. It has no read timeout on its end of the socket, so it waits between requests for as long as the front end leaves it. A kernel made daemonizable on purpose and then left idle for three minutes between two renders answered the second one from the same session. When a kept-alive kernel does end, it takes the PHP engine and the watchdog process that guards it with it, leaving nothing running.

title: Quarto
text:
Freeze
freeze works unchanged, because it is Quarto’s own cache of a cell’s output and the kernel is not involved in it.
execute:
  freeze: auto
With freeze: auto a document is re-executed only when its source changes, which is the setting a documentation site wants: a contributor without PHP 8.5 and the phpstats packages installed can still build the site from the frozen output. The frozen output lives in _freeze/ and is committed.
Quarto resolves a document’s kernel by name while it builds the site navigation, which happens before it reads anything frozen, so a kernelspec of that name has to exist even though nothing starts it. scripts/render-docs --frozen writes one whose command exits as soon as it is started, so a cell that did reach execution fails the render rather than coming out unexecuted. That is how this repository rebuilds its own site with no PHP on the machine.

title: Quarto
text:
Projects
In a Quarto project the kernel is named per document, in each document’s front matter. A project with more than three documents to render turns the daemon off unless --execute-daemon was passed on the command line, which for PHP changes nothing.
One thing is worth checking in a project: Quarto runs the kernel with the document’s own directory as its working directory, and the engine finds the project to load by walking up from there looking for vendor/autoload.php. A document in a subdirectory of a Composer project therefore sees that project. A document outside any Composer project sees none, and JUPHYTER_AUTOLOAD or an autoload entry in a juphyter.json beside the document names one outright.

title: JupyterLab
text:
Once juphyter install has written a kernelspec, JupyterLab lists it in the launcher under the name --display-name gave it, or the name the install command chose by itself. A new notebook with that kernel runs PHP cells.
The kernel has to be installed where the running JupyterLab looks. juphyter install writes to JUPYTER_DATA_DIR when it is set, and otherwise to the per-user data directory, which is ~/Library/Jupyter on macOS and ~/.local/share/jupyter on Linux. jupyter kernelspec list shows what a JupyterLab will find.

title: JupyterLab
text:
What a notebook shows
A cell’s result appears under it as an Out[n]. State carries from one cell to the next, the stop button interrupts a running cell, and restarting the kernel starts a new PHP session with nothing bound.
Tab completion covers three things: the session’s variables after a $, the declared functions and classes for a bare prefix, and a value’s public members after -> or ::. The continuation prompt works as well, so an unterminated block or string leaves the cell open rather than running it.

title: JupyterLab
text:
Plots
JupyterLab draws a phiz plot from the Vega-Lite specification. juphyter publishes the specification under application/vnd.vegalite.v5+json, which is the newest Vega-Lite MIME type JupyterLab’s bundled renderer defines, and the specification itself is Vega-Lite 6.
Publishing a version 6 specification under the version 5 MIME type was the one display risk worth checking before relying on it, because the renderer could reject a construct it does not know. It does not: JupyterLab’s bundled Vega-Lite 5.6.1 compiled sixteen phiz-generated specifications without complaint. No mime-renderer extension is needed, and phiz needs no change.
The static SVG that juphyter also publishes is not JupyterLab’s path. It is there for Quarto’s PDF and docx output and for any front end without JavaScript, and it is the fallback if a later Vega-Lite construct does turn out to be rejected.
The HTML representation is not JupyterLab’s path either. JupyterLab does not execute scripts in text/html output, and phiz’s embed() output is a container plus a script tag, so it would render as an empty box. Quarto’s HTML output is what that representation is for.

title: JupyterLab
text:
Tables
A phibble data frame renders as an HTML table. The table’s own style block uses JupyterLab’s CSS variables for its fonts and colors, with plain fallbacks, so it follows the light and dark themes rather than fighting them.

DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['front end' => 'JupyterLab', 'plot from' => 'the Vega-Lite spec', 'table from' => 'text/html'],
    ['front end' => 'Quarto HTML', 'plot from' => 'the HTML embed', 'table from' => 'text/html'],
    ['front end' => 'Quarto PDF', 'plot from' => 'the static SVG', 'table from' => 'the parsed table'],
]);

title: JupyterLab
text:
Notebooks and projects
Jupyter starts a kernel with the notebook’s own directory as its working directory, and the engine walks up from there looking for vendor/autoload.php. A notebook saved inside a Composer project therefore has that project’s classes in scope, including its phibble and phiz, with nothing to configure.
A notebook kept outside the project it works on needs the autoloader named. JUPHYTER_AUTOLOAD names one for a launch, juphyter install --autoload names one for a kernelspec, and an autoload entry in a juphyter.json beside the notebook names one for a project. A juphyter.json can also set the memory limit and add to the include path:
{
  "autoload": "../app/vendor/autoload.php",
  "memory_limit": "512M",
  "include_path": "lib"
}

title: JupyterLab
text:
Converting a notebook
quarto convert turns a .ipynb into a .qmd and back, and nbconvert exports a notebook to HTML or PDF from Python. Both work on a PHP notebook without knowing anything about PHP, because what they read is the notebook format rather than the language. Quarto covers rendering a document directly.

title: juphyter
text:
juphyter runs PHP in a notebook cell. It installs a Jupyter kernel, so JupyterLab lists PHP in its launcher and Quarto executes {php} blocks in a .qmd. The value a cell returns gets the richest representation the front end can draw: a phibble data frame becomes an HTML table, a phiz plot becomes a chart or a static figure, and everything else gets a compact dump.
A notebook sees the project it sits in. The engine walks up from the notebook’s directory looking for vendor/autoload.php, so a notebook inside a Composer project has that project’s packages and its own classes in scope with no configuration.
$mpg = DataFrame::fromRows(Datasets::mpg());

$mpg
    |> group_by('class')
    |> summarise(models: n(), hwy: mean('hwy'))
    |> arrange(desc('hwy'));

title: juphyter
text:
Install
composer require --dev phpstats/juphyter
vendor/bin/juphyter install
The install command writes one kernelspec where Jupyter looks for them and prints where it went. It needs a Python installation that has ipykernel, because the kernel is a Python transport in front of a PHP engine, and it reports the exact pip command when that is missing. Several PHP versions can be installed side by side, each under its own --name.
Static images from phiz plots need the vl-convert binary on PATH. Without it a plot still draws in HTML output and in JupyterLab, and a PDF has no figure to place.

title: juphyter
text:
What it covers

A Jupyter kernel for PHP 8.3 and later, on macOS and Linux.
State across cells, so a variable bound in one cell is in scope in the next.
Tracebacks that name the cell and the line a stack frame came from, rather than eval()'d code.
Rich display for phibble tables and phiz plots, with toMimeBundle() and toHtml() hooks for any other class.
Completion, is_complete for a front end’s continuation prompt, and interruption through the stop button.
Quarto’s .qmd and JupyterLab, with cell options, figure captions, and HTML, ipynb, and PDF output.

title: juphyter
text:
The phpstats family
juphyter is the notebook of the phpstats family. phibble provides data frames, phplyr the dplyr verbs over them, phiz the plots, and phit and CmdStanPHP the models. juphyter requires none of them and formats any of them that is installed.
Get started walks through a first notebook. Quarto covers rendering a document, and JupyterLab covers the notebook interface.

title: Get started
text:
A kernelspec belongs to the machine, so the usual choice is to install juphyter once for your user, as Installation describes. Installing it as a development dependency of one project pins the kernel’s version with that project, at the cost of a kernelspec that names that project’s copy of the engine:
composer require --dev phpstats/juphyter
vendor/bin/juphyter install
The command prints what the kernel is made of.
Installed the juphyter kernel "php" for PHP 8.5.10.
  kernel.json  /Users/you/Library/Jupyter/kernels/php/kernel.json
  python       /opt/homebrew/bin/python3 (ipykernel 7.4.0)
  php          /opt/homebrew/bin/php
  engine       /path/to/vendor/phpstats/juphyter/bin/juphyter
  quarto       /opt/homebrew/bin/python3 (jupyter_client 8.10.0)
The Python is the interpreter that owns the jupyter on PATH, because the kernel runs inside it. --python names a different one. The PHP is the binary that runs the cells, and --php names a different one, which is how several versions coexist:
vendor/bin/juphyter install --name php83 --php /opt/homebrew/opt/php@8.3/bin/php
vendor/bin/juphyter install --name php85 --php /opt/homebrew/opt/php@8.5/bin/php
juphyter uninstall --name php83 removes a kernelspec juphyter wrote, and refuses to remove one it did not.
The quarto line appears when Quarto is installed. Quarto runs an interpreter of its own choosing, and that one is the one that needs Jupyter in it, so the line reports which interpreter that is and what was found there. When it says (no Jupyter), the kernelspec is still correct and quarto render cannot reach it; Installation covers the fix.
On a machine with no Python that can host the kernel at all, the command offers to build one. Installation covers that and the --create-venv option that answers the offer in advance.

text:
Where to go next
Quarto covers rendering a .qmd to HTML, ipynb, and PDF. JupyterLab covers the notebook interface and what it draws.

title: Installation
text:
juphyter has two halves. The engine that runs your cells is PHP, and the transport that speaks the Jupyter protocol is a small Python module that runs inside ipykernel. Installing juphyter means putting a kernelspec where Jupyter looks for one, pointing at both.
A kernelspec belongs to the machine rather than to a project. There is one php kernel per user, whatever directory you installed from, so installing juphyter once for your user is the usual choice. The engine does not need to live in a project either: it starts in the document’s own directory and walks up for a vendor/autoload.php, so a document anywhere on disk gets a working PHP kernel.

title: Installation
text:
Requirements

PHP 8.3 or later, from Homebrew, Herd, or a distribution package. That floor matches phibble and phplyr. phiz needs PHP 8.5, so plots are available only on a kernel running 8.5 or newer.
Composer.
Python 3 with jupyter and ipykernel 7.0 or later. The wrapper subclasses ipykernel.kernelbase.Kernel, which changed in version 7. This costs nothing extra in practice: JupyterLab is a Python application, and Quarto’s jupyter engine requires a Python Jupyter whatever kernel it drives.
Quarto, to render Quarto documents.
macOS or Linux. The kernel interrupts a running cell with POSIX signals, which the Windows PHP build does not provide.

pcntl is wanted rather than required. Without it the kernel runs and the stop button does nothing, so juphyter install checks the PHP binary it is about to name and says so rather than refusing to install.

title: Installation
text:
Install
Copy the whole block:
# Does the Python that Quarto will use already have Jupyter?
py="$(command -v python3)"
"$py" -c 'import jupyter_client' 2>/dev/null || py=''

# juphyter. It is not on Packagist yet, so Composer reads the repository
# directly, which "no-api" does over git and without a GitHub token.
composer global config repositories.juphyter \
  '{"type":"vcs","url":"https://github.com/phpstats/juphyter","no-api":true}'
composer global require phpstats/juphyter:dev-main

# The juphyter command on PATH.
bin="$(composer global config bin-dir --absolute 2>/dev/null)"
export PATH="$bin:$PATH"
grep -qF "$bin" ~/.zshrc 2>/dev/null \
  || echo "export PATH=\"$bin:\$PATH\"" >> ~/.zshrc

# Jupyter, in a virtual environment, only when that Python has none. Quarto
# picks it up as the python3 on PATH.
if [ -z "$py" ]; then
  python3 -m venv ~/.venvs/juphyter
  ~/.venvs/juphyter/bin/pip install jupyterlab
  export PATH="$HOME/.venvs/juphyter/bin:$PATH"
  grep -qF '.venvs/juphyter/bin' ~/.zshrc 2>/dev/null \
    || echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.venvs/juphyter/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.zshrc
  py="$HOME/.venvs/juphyter/bin/python"
fi

# The kernelspec, naming that Python and the PHP on PATH.
juphyter install --python "$py"

# Check. It reports what it found and fails if anything is broken.
juphyter doctor
On a machine running bash, write ~/.bashrc in place of ~/.zshrc.
juphyter install prints where the kernelspec went, which Python, PHP, and engine it recorded, and which Python Quarto appears to use:
Installed the juphyter kernel "php" for PHP 8.5.10.
  kernel.json  /Users/you/Library/Jupyter/kernels/php/kernel.json
  python       /Users/you/.venvs/juphyter/bin/python (ipykernel 7.4.0)
  php          /opt/homebrew/bin/php
  engine       /Users/you/.composer/vendor/phpstats/juphyter/bin/juphyter
  quarto       /Users/you/.venvs/juphyter/bin/python (jupyter_client 8.10.0)
If ipykernel is missing from that interpreter the command writes nothing and prints the pip install line that fixes it. The interpreter it picks is the one that owns the jupyter on your PATH, read from that script’s shebang, because that is the environment your Jupyter actually runs in. Use --python to name a different one.
The quarto line is a different question from the python line above, and the command reports it rather than acting on it. The line is absent when quarto is not on your PATH. When the interpreter Quarto will run has no Jupyter in it, the line says so and the command prints a warning naming the PATH entry that fixes it:
  quarto       /opt/homebrew/opt/python@3.14/bin/python3.14 (no Jupyter)
The kernelspec is still written and the command still exits 0, because a kernel Quarto cannot reach is a working JupyterLab kernel. quarto check jupyter is the authority on which interpreter Quarto chose, and the section below explains the failure the warning is about.

Why the kernel is installed against Quarto’s Python
Quarto chooses its own Python, independently of the one that installed the kernel, and the interpreter it chooses is the one that has to have Jupyter, because Jupyter is what starts the kernel and collects its output. On a typical macOS machine the python3 on PATH is a Homebrew build with no Jupyter in it, and quarto render then fails on a document whose kernel is installed and working:
ERROR: Jupyter kernel 'php' not found. Known kernels: python3
The install block asks that interpreter for jupyter_client before anything else and names it in --python when it has it, so Quarto and the kernelspec agree on one Python and nothing needs overriding. When it has no Jupyter, the block builds a virtual environment and puts it first on PATH, where Quarto finds it as python3.
quarto check jupyter reports the interpreter Quarto chose, whether it has Jupyter, and the kernels it can see through it:
Path: /Users/you/.venvs/juphyter/bin/python
Jupyter: 5.9.1
Kernels: php, python3
A Jupyter: (None) line there is this failure, whatever jupyter kernelspec list reports. The kernel is not the problem in that case, and the kernelspec needs no reinstall. quarto check writes its report to standard error, so pipe it through 2>&1 before a grep.
In VS Code or Positron, the interpreter selected for the workspace is the one Quarto receives, so an error that survives an otherwise correct install usually means that selection names an interpreter with no Jupyter in it.
QUARTO_PYTHON names an interpreter outright, for one shell or one project. Quarto reads it from the environment first, then from a project _environment file beside _quarto.yml, and falls back to the first python3 on PATH. The file cannot override a variable the environment already carries, which is what makes the editor’s selection decisive: the Quarto extension sets QUARTO_PYTHON from it on every render, so a wrong selection is corrected through the interpreter picker and not through a file.
Exporting it from a shell startup file is worth avoiding, because it takes precedence over an activated virtual environment and would therefore change the interpreter for every Quarto project on the machine.


When no Python can host the kernel
The kernelspec names an interpreter with ipykernel 7 or newer, and a machine whose only Python is the system or a Homebrew build has none. Those builds are marked externally managed, so pip install into them refuses, which leaves a virtual environment as the supported way out.
juphyter install offers to build one when it finds no interpreter that works:
Build a virtual environment with jupyterlab at /Users/you/.venvs/juphyter and
install the kernel into it? [y/N]
--create-venv PATH answers that in advance, which is what a script or a CI job needs:
juphyter install --create-venv ~/.venvs/juphyter
The environment gets jupyterlab, which carries the ipykernel the kernelspec names and the jupyter_client that Quarto starts a kernel through, so one environment answers both. An environment already at that path is adopted rather than rebuilt, and the packages are installed either way, so a second run finishes an interrupted one. A directory that exists and holds something else is refused rather than written into.
Pointing Quarto at the environment is still yours to do, and the command prints how. With no terminal to put the question to, the environment is built without asking: there is nobody there to answer, and it is written under your home directory without touching any interpreter that was already on the machine.
An explicit --python turns the offer off. Naming an interpreter is a decision about which one to use, and building a different one would answer a question you did not ask.


Pointing Quarto at the environment
A new environment is of no use to Quarto until Quarto runs it. In Positron, VS Code, or Cursor, select it for the workspace with Python: Select Interpreter. The Quarto extension hands the workspace interpreter to Quarto for every render in that workspace, so no other project changes.
At a terminal, activate it for the shell:
source ~/.venvs/juphyter/bin/activate
juphyter writes nothing to a shell startup file. An entry in one would change python3 for every Quarto project on the machine, which is the harm that keeps QUARTO_PYTHON out of a startup file as well.

title: Installation
text:
Checking an install later
juphyter install reports what it recorded at the moment it recorded it, and everything it names can move afterwards. A brew upgrade replaces the PHP binary a kernelspec points at, a deleted project takes the engine inside its vendor directory, a removed virtual environment takes the interpreter, and a new terminal can carry a PATH that no longer reaches the Jupyter the kernel was installed against. Each of those leaves a kernel that a front end lists and cannot start, and none of them changes the kernelspec.
juphyter doctor asks those questions and changes nothing:
juphyter doctor

This package
  ok    the Python wrapper is at /Users/you/.composer/vendor/.../kernel

PHP
  ok    PHP 8.5.10 at /opt/homebrew/bin/php
  ok    pcntl is there, so the stop button interrupts a cell

A Python for the kernel
  ok    /Users/you/.venvs/juphyter/bin/python has ipykernel 7.4.0

Quarto
  fail  quarto will run /opt/homebrew/bin/python3.14, which has no Jupyter

Kernels in /Users/you/Library/Jupyter/kernels
  ok    php is complete
  fail  php83: its PHP /opt/homebrew/Cellar/php/8.3.1/bin/php does not run

JupyterLab: ready, with php.
Quarto: not ready.
The PATH entry it suggests comes from an interpreter it has just confirmed has ipykernel, which is a kernel’s own interpreter when the one a fresh install would pick no longer works. It is printed twice, as an export for the shell you are in and as the append that keeps it, because the first alone lasts only until that shell closes. --prefix looks under a prefix rather than the per-user directory, and the exit code is 1 when anything is broken, so a script can ask.
A kernel juphyter did not write is left out of the report, as juphyter uninstall refuses to remove one.

title: Installation
text:
Your first Quarto document
Write a document in any directory, with no project around it:
---
title: "PHP in Quarto"
jupyter: php
---

::: {#3313d2a6 .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.php .cell-code}
echo "sum: ", array_sum(range(1, 10)), "\n";
PHP_VERSION;
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
sum: 55
```
:::

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1}
```
'8.5.10'
```
:::
:::

quarto render hello.qmd runs the cell and puts its output in the HTML. Cell options work as they do for any other engine, because PHP accepts # comments.
In JupyterLab, started with jupyter lab, the same kernel appears in the launcher under the PHP version it found.

title: Installation
text:
Checking it worked
juphyter doctor
It names what it found and says which front ends work. Checking an install later covers the report and what each finding means. jupyter kernelspec list is the narrower question of whether Jupyter can see the kernelspec at all.

title: Installation
text:
The phpstats packages
None of them is a dependency of juphyter, which installs and runs with any subset of the family present, including none of it. The install above therefore runs plain PHP, and phibble tables and phiz plots need the packages added.
A second kernel gives them to a document in any directory:
for r in phibble phplyr; do
  composer global config "repositories.$r" \
    "{\"type\":\"vcs\",\"url\":\"https://github.com/phpstats/$r\",\"no-api\":true}"
done
composer global require --prefer-source "phpstats/phibble:^0.3" "phpstats/phplyr:^0.3"

juphyter install --name phpstats --display-name "PHP (phpstats)" \
  --autoload "$(composer global config home 2>/dev/null)/vendor/autoload.php"
Name that kernel in the front matter as jupyter: phpstats.
It is a second kernel rather than a change to the first because --autoload fixes one autoloader for every document it runs, which suits a document outside any project and breaks one inside a project. The php kernel keeps the default search described under Which dependencies a notebook sees, so a document inside a Composer project sees that project’s own packages.
The packages are not on Packagist, so each needs a repositories entry with "no-api": true, which makes Composer read the repository with git rather than through the GitHub API and so needs no token. --prefer-source is needed for the same reason, because a dist zipball still comes from the API.
Use the released ^0.3 tags rather than dev-main for these. phplyr requires phpstats/phibble ^0.3, which a dev-main phibble does not satisfy, so asking for dev-main on both fails to resolve.
phiz requires PHP 8.5 and has to be left out below that. On 8.5 or newer, add it with composer global require --prefer-source "phpstats/phiz:^0.3".

title: Installation
text:
Inside a single project
Installing juphyter as a project dependency pins the kernel’s version with the project:
composer require --dev phpstats/juphyter
vendor/bin/juphyter install
The kernelspec it writes is still the machine’s, and it names that project’s copy of the engine. Two consequences follow. Running the same command from a second project replaces the first kernelspec, which juphyter install reports as Replaced, and deleting the project’s vendor directory leaves every notebook on the machine pointing at an engine that is gone. Give each project’s kernel its own --name to keep them apart.

title: Installation
text:
Without Composer: the standalone PHAR
A standalone PHAR gives you a kernel on a machine with no Composer:
php juphyter.phar install
The kernelspec then names the PHAR as its engine, and the engine finds a project’s dependencies at run time by walking up from the notebook’s own directory. A PHAR install also copies the Python wrapper out of the archive and beside the kernelspec, because Python cannot import from inside a phar:// path.

title: Installation
text:
Several PHP versions at once
Each kernel needs its own name, and the display name follows the version it finds:
juphyter install --name php83 --php /path/to/php83
juphyter install --name php85 --php /path/to/php85
That produces two kernels in the launcher, “PHP 8.3” and “PHP 8.5”. Pass --display-name to label them yourself.
An absolute --php path is recorded as you wrote it. That matters with Homebrew, where resolving the symlink would pin the kernelspec to a versioned path such as /opt/homebrew/Cellar/php/8.5.10/bin/php that brew upgrade removes. A bare name such as php8.4 is still resolved to an absolute path, since a kernelspec cannot rely on your PATH.

title: Installation
text:
Where the kernelspec goes
juphyter install writes to the per-user Jupyter data directory, which is ~/Library/Jupyter/kernels on macOS and $XDG_DATA_HOME/jupyter/kernels or ~/.local/share/jupyter/kernels on Linux. JUPYTER_DATA_DIR and JUPYTER_PLATFORM_DIRS are both honored, as jupyter --paths reports them. --prefix PATH writes under PATH/share/jupyter instead, which is the layout jupyter kernelspec install --prefix produces.
juphyter uninstall removes a kernelspec, and only one that juphyter wrote. It refuses to delete somebody else’s kernel of the same name, as does a reinstall.

title: Installation
text:
Which dependencies a notebook sees
The engine starts in the notebook’s own directory, walks up looking for vendor/autoload.php, and loads the first one it finds. A notebook anywhere inside a Composer project therefore sees that project’s packages with no configuration.
Two ways to override that search, and the most explicit one wins. JUPHYTER_AUTOLOAD in the environment comes first, which is what --autoload at install time records in the kernelspec. A juphyter.json beside the notebook, or anywhere above it, comes second, and can set the same thing along with two run-time settings:
{
  "autoload": "vendor/autoload.php",
  "memory_limit": "512M",
  "include_path": "lib"
}
Relative paths in that file resolve against the file’s own directory, so one juphyter.json at a project’s root serves every notebook beneath it.

title: Installation
text:
Static images
Plots render as interactive charts in JupyterLab and in Quarto’s HTML output with nothing else installed. Rendering a Quarto document to PDF or Word needs a static image, which phiz produces with the vl-convert binary. Put it on your PATH, or name it in PHIZ_VL_CONVERT. Without it, a plot in a PDF falls back to its text description.
The Python package vl-convert-python is not a substitute: it ships a library and no executable, and phiz runs the binary.
Either override replaces the search rather than extending it. A kernel installed with --autoload loads that one autoloader for every notebook it runs, including a notebook that sits inside a Composer project of its own, so keep such a kernel under its own --name as The phpstats packages does.

title: Limitations
text: Some of these follow from PHP itself and will not change. Others are milestone boundaries and will. Each one says which.

title: Limitations
section: A cell cannot redeclare a class or a function
text:
A cell cannot redeclare a class or a function
PHP has no way to replace a class, interface, trait, enum, or function once it is declared, so re-running a cell that declares one cannot work. The kernel refuses such a cell before executing anything, naming the collision:
RedeclarationError: The class, interface, trait or enum "Widget" was already
declared in this session, and PHP cannot redeclare it. Restart the kernel to
redefine it.
Refusing is deliberate. Letting it reach eval() would be an uncatchable fatal error that ends the kernel rather than an error the notebook can show.
The session records a name only once PHP really holds it, so a cell that failed to declare anything leaves the name free. class Widget extends Typo {} throws and declares nothing, and the corrected cell runs. The common case this serves is running cells out of order: define a base class after its subclass, run the subclass cell first, then run them in the right order, and it works.
A conditional declaration is not affected, because PHP does not bind one at compile time:
if (! function_exists('helper')) {
    function helper() { /* ... */ }
}
This follows from PHP and will not change.

title: Limitations
section: A cell cannot declare a namespace
text:
A cell cannot declare a namespace
A namespace declaration is refused. Changing namespace part way through a session breaks name resolution for everything already defined, and the kernel would have no honest way to decide which namespace a later cell belongs to. Use fully qualified names, or use statements, which do carry from one cell to the next.
This is a deliberate refusal and is not planned to change.

title: Limitations
section: Every cell runs under strict types
text:
Every cell runs under strict types
The kernel prepends declare(strict_types=1); to each cell, because PHP accepts that declaration nowhere but the first statement. A cell writing it for itself is fine and the kernel removes the duplicate. declare(strict_types=0) is refused, since the kernel cannot honor it, and so is declare(encoding=...), which has the same first-statement rule. declare(ticks=...) is left alone.

title: Limitations
section: References and $this do not survive between cells
text:
References and $this do not survive between cells
Variables are carried across cells by value. A reference taken in one cell is an ordinary copy in the next, and $this has no meaning at a notebook’s top level. Objects, arrays, scalars, and resources all persist normally. Every PHP REPL behaves this way.

title: Limitations
section: A closure called from another cell has no line in its traceback
text:
A closure called from another cell has no line in its traceback
A traceback names the cell and the line for ordinary functions and methods, across cells:
RuntimeException: from the function
  at Cell 1, line 3, in boom()
  at Cell 2, line 2
A closure is different. PHP’s trace does not say where a closure was declared, and every cell’s eval() shares one file name, so a closure declared in one cell and called from another cannot be placed. The kernel reports the stack frame without a location rather than guessing:
LogicException: from the closure
  in a closure
  at Cell 4, line 4
Naming a line it could not know would send you to the wrong place, which is worse than naming none. The call site is still reported. This is a milestone boundary.

title: Limitations
section: A cell whose value is null shows no output
text:
A cell whose value is null shows no output
var_dump($x);, Juphyter\display($df), and any other call that returns nothing produce no Out[N], the same way a Python notebook shows nothing for None. Every other value is shown, including 0, false, '', [], and 'null'.

title: Limitations
section: A cell that calls exit or die ends the kernel
text:
A cell that calls exit or die ends the kernel
PHP cannot catch either, so the process goes. The kernel reports it rather than disappearing silently:
SystemExit: The cell ended the kernel process with exit or die, so nothing
further can run. Restart the kernel to carry on.
Anything the cell printed first is still shown. This follows from PHP.

title: Limitations
section: Interrupting needs pcntl, and a cell can still swallow it
text:
Interrupting needs pcntl, and a cell can still swallow it
The stop button sends a signal, so the PHP binary running cells needs the pcntl extension with its functions callable. juphyter install checks the binary it names and warns when it cannot signal, including the case where the extension is loaded but its functions sit in disable_functions.
An interrupt arrives as Juphyter\Engine\Interrupt, which extends Error rather than Exception so that ordinary defensive code does not absorb it. A cell that catches Throwable in a loop can still swallow it, which is the same trade Python makes by putting KeyboardInterrupt outside Exception.

title: Limitations
section: A data frame’s numbers in an HTML table are not pillar’s
text:
A data frame’s numbers in an HTML table are not pillar’s
A data frame’s text/plain output is phibble’s own, character for character. The HTML table is the kernel’s, and it formats a float with PHP’s own string conversion rather than reproducing pillar’s significant-figure logic, so a wide dbl column can read differently in the two. The HTML header also omits the group count that the text output carries. Both are milestone boundaries.

title: Limitations
text:
macOS and Linux only
The kernel interrupts a cell with POSIX signals and reaps a child process, which the Windows PHP build does not support. This matches the platforms the phit and phpolars extensions declare.

title: Limitations
text:
Not yet implemented
These are milestone boundaries with nothing in the design against them:

Documentation on hover. Jupyter’s inspect_request is not answered, so shift-tab shows nothing.
Reading input. A cell cannot prompt, so readline() and fgets(STDIN) have nothing to read.
Magics. There are no %-prefixed commands.
Widgets. ipywidgets is not supported.
The debugger. Jupyter’s debug protocol is not implemented, so JupyterLab’s debugger does not attach.
A Vega-Lite 6 renderer. phiz emits Vega-Lite 6 and JupyterLab’s bundled renderer reads version 5, so plots are published under the version 5 MIME type. Everything phiz currently produces compiles under the renderer JupyterLab ships, and the static SVG covers anything that does not.
